analysis.one_liner: Pays landowners when federal rules cut their property's value by 20% or more.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote; after referral to the Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee in March 2000, it sat until Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the federal government to pay landowners whenever an agency action under four environmental laws — the Clean Water Act's wetlands program, the Endangered Species Act, the swampbuster farm program, and federal reclamation and land-use laws — cut their property's value by 20% or more. If the loss exceeded 50%, the government would have to buy the land at full market value at the owner's request. Payments would come out of the regulating agency's own budget, and owners could take disputed claims to binding arbitration or court with taxpayers covering their attorney fees and appraisal costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of land regulated under the Endangered Species Act, federal wetlands rules, the farm swampbuster program, or federal water-rights laws. Because compensation is proportional to lost market value, the largest payouts would go to owners of the most valuable regulated land — developers, large landholders, and agricultural operators. Owners whose land lost more than half its value could also sell it to the government at full price.

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal payment to any landowner whose property value drops 20% or more because of an agency action under the Clean Water Act's wetlands program, the Endangered Species Act, the swampbuster program, or federal reclamation and land-management laws [S2][S3].
If a regulation cuts a property's value by more than 50%, the owner can force the government to buy that portion at full fair market value [S2][S3].

Gives owners a choice between binding arbitration and a lawsuit, and requires the government to pay the owner's attorney fees, arbitration costs, and appraisal fees if the owner prevails, plus interest from the date of the restriction [S3].
Requires agencies to notify affected owners of their compensation rights whenever an action limits property use [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally. Every compensation payment, buyout, arbitration award, and prevailing owner's legal fees would be charged to the annual appropriation of the agency that issued the rule — the same budget that funds the agency's work — with agencies authorized to transfer or reprogram funds to cover judgments [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compensation and buyouts would be paid from the regulating agency's own annual appropriation, so the cost of paying landowners would compete directly with the agency's enforcement and program budget [S3].

The compensation requirement applies to actions under the Endangered Species Act and federal wetlands protections, so agencies would face a fiscal price for protecting habitat and wetlands, which could make those protections harder to apply [S2][S3].
Any payment obligation is 'subject to the availability of appropriations,' meaning owners would hold a claim the government could still fail to fund in a given year [S3].

The bill carves out some limits: no compensation for actions whose main purpose is preventing a public health or safety hazard or damage to other property, no compensation for uses that are nuisances or already prohibited by local zoning, and no compensation under the navigational servitude except for wetlands [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Paying owners when the government regulates land has a fairness logic — the same people bear a burden for a public benefit. But the bill's design would have made environmental protection expensive in a way that fell on the agencies doing the protecting, with compensation scaled to land value so the largest checks would flow to the owners of the most valuable regulated land. Its carve-outs for health and safety and nuisances limited but did not eliminate the fiscal burden, and its appropriations proviso made payment uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee when introduced, then to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee in March 2000, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Tom DeLay introduced the bill on July 19, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
Thirty-seven members cosponsored the bill — 35 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S4].
On March 27, 2000, eight months after introduction, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill died at the subcommittee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and the agencies administering wetlands and endangered-species rules were better off, since no compensation obligation was created. Owners of regulated land who would have filed claims never received the payments the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Private Property Protection Act of 1999 and recruited 37 cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup, and referred the bill to a subcommittee in March 2000 where it sat until Congress ended.

against.name: Environmental organizations
against.what_they_did: Organized opposition to property-rights compensation legislation in this era on the ground that it would make wetlands and endangered-species protections too costly for agencies to enforce.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 35 of 37 cosponsors were Republicans, with 2 Democrats — and no vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landholders
industries.note: The bill would have paid them cash whenever federal rules cut their land's value by 20% or more, with buyouts at full price above 50%, financed by taxpayers. Because compensation scales with lost market value, the biggest checks would have gone to the owners of the most valuable regulated land.

Owners of farmland affected by the swampbuster program, the Endangered Species Act, or federal reclamation water rights would have gained a right to compensation. Smaller family operations would have benefited alongside large ones, but taxpayers — including farmers — would have funded the payments.

The bill would have charged every compensation payment and legal fee to the issuing agency's own budget, raising the fiscal cost of protecting wetlands and endangered species and giving agencies an incentive to avoid restrictions that trigger claims. The exception for public health and safety actions left some authority intact.
